posts.title: Agent demos vs agent production
posts.hook: Every agent demo I've seen this month nails the happy path. Zero of them show what happens at step 47 when the context window is 80% full and the model starts hallucinating tool calls.
posts.body:
Every agent demo I've seen this month nails the happy path. Zero of them show what happens at step 47 when the context window is 80% full and the model starts hallucinating tool calls.

I run multi-step agent workflows daily. Enrichment chains, scraping pipelines, CRM hydration. The failure mode is never "the model is dumb." It's always one of three things:

1. Context got too fat and the model lost the thread
2. A tool returned unexpected output and the agent kept going instead of stopping
3. The plan was fine but the execution order was wrong

The fix isn't better models. It's better scaffolding. Checkpoints after every tool call. Context compression between steps. Hard stops when output shape doesn't match expectations.

I've started treating agent runs like plumbing jobs. You don't snake the whole line hoping it works. You isolate sections, test pressure, confirm flow, then move to the next joint.

The teams shipping real agent workflows aren't chasing autonomy. They're building guardrails that make autonomy safe.
posts.cta: What's the weirdest failure mode you've hit running agents in production?

remixes.label: autopsy-report
remixes.hook: I killed a production agent workflow last Tuesday. Not on purpose. It drowned in its own context.
remixes.body:
I killed a production agent workflow last Tuesday. Not on purpose. It drowned in its own context.

Here's the autopsy. I had a 50-step enrichment chain pulling company data, matching contacts, scoring fit, and writing to CRM. Steps 1 through 35 ran clean. Then the agent started calling tools that didn't exist. Not random hallucinations. It was mixing up tool names from earlier in the conversation with ones it encountered later. The context window was so bloated it couldn't distinguish step 12's output from step 42's instructions.

Three things I changed after that failure:

First, I started compressing context aggressively between phases. Each phase gets a summary, not the raw output. The agent works from the summary going forward.

Second, I added hard checkpoints. Every 15 steps, the workflow writes state to disk and can restart from that checkpoint with a clean context.

Third, I stopped trusting the agent to know when it's confused. I validate tool call schemas before execution. If the agent calls a tool with wrong parameters, it gets a structured error instead of a hallucinated result.

The gap between demo agents and production agents is error handling. Demos show what the model can do. Production shows what happens when the model fails, and whether your system recovers.
remixes.cta: What's your checkpoint strategy for long-running agent workflows?

remixes.label: industry-blindspot
remixes.hook: The agent framework market is selling Act 1 of a three-act play. Nobody's buying tickets for Acts 2 and 3, where things actually get hard.
remixes.body:
The agent framework market is selling Act 1 of a three-act play. Nobody's buying tickets for Acts 2 and 3, where things actually get hard.

Act 1 is the demo. Clean input, happy path, perfect output. Five tool calls, maybe ten. The model looks brilliant. This is what gets funding rounds closed and Twitter threads viral.

Act 2 is integration. Your agent needs to talk to six different APIs, handle rate limits, manage auth tokens, retry on failures, and not lose its place when one service goes down. Most frameworks punt on this entirely.

Act 3 is degradation. What happens at scale. When the context window fills up. When the model starts confusing instructions from step 5 with data from step 30. When a tool returns unexpected output and the agent tries to parse it anyway, cascading errors through every downstream step.

I've shipped all three acts. The lesson is simple. The model is rarely the bottleneck. The orchestration layer is. How you manage context, how you handle partial failures, how you checkpoint and resume. That's the real engineering.

If your agent framework doesn't have a story for Act 3, you don't have a production framework. You have a demo kit.

I run multi-step agent workflows daily. Enrichment chains, scraping pipelines, CRM hydration. Here's what I'd tell any team moving agents from prototype to production: the failure mode is never "the model is dumb." It's predictable and preventable.

The three failure patterns I see repeatedly:

First, context bloat. Every tool call appends tokens. By step 40, the model is re-reading thousands of irrelevant tokens on every inference. Solution: compress aggressively between phases. Summarize, don't append.

Second, tool schema drift. The model starts hallucinating tool parameters that worked earlier but aren't valid in the current step. Solution: validate every tool call against a strict schema before execution. Reject bad calls with structured errors.

Third, state confusion. The model loses track of which step it's on and starts repeating work or skipping steps. Solution: external state management. Don't rely on the model to track its own progress. Write checkpoints to disk.

My recommendation: before scaling any agent workflow past 20 steps, instrument it. Log every tool call, every context size, every token count. The data will show you exactly where your workflow breaks before your users do.

posts.title: Mandating AI tools without context
posts.hook: Mandating AI coding tools company-wide is like mandating everyone use a table saw. Great tool. Also removes fingers if you skip the training.
posts.body:
Mandating AI coding tools company-wide is like mandating everyone use a table saw. Great tool. Also removes fingers if you skip the training.

I've watched three patterns play out when companies force AI tooling:

Pattern 1: Senior devs get frustrated because the tool generates plausible garbage they have to review line by line. Net negative productivity.

Pattern 2: Junior devs accept AI output uncritically. Code works on the surface, breaks in production. Technical debt compounds silently.

Pattern 3: A small group figures out how to actually use it. They build custom instructions, feed it real context, treat it like a junior dev who needs precise direction. They ship 3x faster.

The difference between pattern 1 and pattern 3 isn't the tool. It's whether anyone bothered to teach context engineering before flipping the switch.

I use Claude Code for 6+ hours a day. It's the backbone of everything I build. But I also spent months learning how to feed it context, when to trust it, and when to override it.

The mandate isn't the problem. The absence of craft is.
posts.cta: If your company rolled out AI tools, did they invest in training or just flip a switch?

remixes.label: training-gap-playbook
remixes.hook: The company that gave every developer Copilot and no training saw a 15% increase in bugs merged to main within six weeks. The company that trained first saw a 30% reduction. Same tool.
remixes.body:
The company that gave every developer Copilot and no training saw a 15% increase in bugs merged to main within six weeks. The company that trained first saw a 30% reduction. Same tool.

I've been consulting on AI tool rollouts for months now. The pattern is so consistent it's boring.

Companies that flip the switch without training get three outcomes. Senior engineers waste time reviewing AI-generated code that looks right but has subtle bugs. Junior engineers ship code they don't understand. And the team builds a collective distrust of the tool that takes months to undo.

Companies that invest two weeks in structured training get different outcomes entirely. They teach engineers what the tool is good at and where it falls apart. They establish review patterns. They build shared prompts and workflows that compound across the team.

The training doesn't need to be elaborate. Three sessions:

Session one: where AI code generation fails. Show real examples of plausible but broken output. Teach engineers to spot the patterns.

Session two: effective prompting for your codebase. Not generic prompt tips. Actual examples using your stack, your conventions, your patterns.

Session three: review workflows. How to efficiently verify AI output without reading every line. What to trust, what to double-check.

Two weeks of training versus six months of cleaning up the mess. The math is obvious.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Hot take: most companies shouldn't mandate AI coding tools at all. They should let the early adopters prove the value, then let adoption spread organically.
remixes.body:
Hot take: most companies shouldn't mandate AI coding tools at all. They should let the early adopters prove the value, then let adoption spread organically.

Mandates create resentment. Developers who are forced to use a tool they didn't choose will find every reason it doesn't work. They'll blame the tool for their own workflow friction. And they won't be entirely wrong, because no tool works well when you're fighting it.

What I've seen work instead:

Find your 2-3 engineers who are already using AI tools on their own time. Give them explicit permission to use them at work. Let them build workflows that actually fit your codebase.

After a month, have them present what they built. Not a vendor demo. Real examples from your actual codebase. The wins AND the failures.

The engineers who are interested will start experimenting. The ones who aren't ready will see what's possible without feeling forced. Within a quarter, you'll have organic adoption at 40-60% without a single mandate.

The remaining 40% who don't adopt? Some of them are right. Not every workflow benefits from AI assistance. Some codebases are too specialized. Some tasks require too much domain context.

Mandates assume the tool is universally valuable. It isn't. Let your team figure out where it actually helps.

posts.title: Context window costs at scale
posts.hook: Ran a 73-step enrichment pipeline last week. The agent worked perfectly for the first 40 steps. Then the context window hit 180K tokens and costs went vertical.
posts.body:
Ran a 73-step enrichment pipeline last week. The agent worked perfectly for the first 40 steps. Then the context window hit 180K tokens and costs went vertical.

The math nobody talks about with agentic workflows: every tool call adds input tokens. Every response adds output tokens. And most agent frameworks just... keep appending. By step 60, the model is re-reading the entire conversation history on every single call.

My fix was ugly but effective. I break long pipelines into phases. Each phase gets a fresh context with a structured handoff doc. Phase 1 does discovery, writes a summary. Phase 2 reads the summary, does enrichment. Phase 3 reads enrichment output, does scoring.

Total cost dropped 4x. Accuracy actually went up because the model wasn't drowning in stale context from 50 steps ago.

This is why I keep everything in SQLite instead of keeping state in the conversation. The database remembers. The agent only loads what it needs for the current step.

Long-running agents aren't a model problem. They're an architecture problem.

remixes.label: cost-autopsy
remixes.hook: My agent workflow costs $0.12 per run now. Three weeks ago it cost $4.80 per run. Same output. Same quality. I just stopped letting the framework waste my money.
remixes.body:
My agent workflow costs $0.12 per run now. Three weeks ago it cost $4.80 per run. Same output. Same quality. I just stopped letting the framework waste my money.

The default behavior of most agent frameworks is to append everything to the conversation. Every tool call input. Every tool call output. Every intermediate reasoning step. By step 30, the model is re-reading a novel-length conversation on every inference.

Here's what I changed:

First, I implemented phase-based context compression. My enrichment pipeline has five phases. At the end of each phase, I summarize the results into a structured object and start the next phase with only that summary. The model never sees raw data from three phases ago.

Second, I switched to smaller models for simple steps. Not every step needs Opus. Data extraction? Haiku handles it fine at 1/30th the cost. I only escalate to the expensive model for reasoning-heavy steps like scoring and recommendations.

Third, I added token budgets per step. If a step exceeds its budget, the workflow pauses and alerts me instead of silently burning tokens. This caught two bugs in my first week. Steps that were looping and re-processing the same data.

The unsexy truth about agent costs: the model pricing isn't the problem. Your architecture is. Fix the architecture and the same workflow that costs $5 runs for pennies.

remixes.label: hidden-math
remixes.hook: Nobody in the agent space talks about input token costs. Everyone talks about output tokens. But on a 70-step workflow, input tokens are 85% of your bill.
remixes.body:
Nobody in the agent space talks about input token costs. Everyone talks about output tokens. But on a 70-step workflow, input tokens are 85% of your bill.

Here's why. Every time the model takes an action, the entire conversation history gets sent as input. On step 1, that's maybe 2K tokens. On step 40, it's 120K tokens. On step 70, it's pushing 200K. And you're paying input token rates on every single one of those tokens, every single step.

I tracked one pipeline across 73 steps last week. The math:

Steps 1-20: 45K cumulative input tokens. Cost: $0.34
Steps 21-40: 280K cumulative input tokens. Cost: $2.10
Steps 41-60: 890K cumulative input tokens. Cost: $6.68
Steps 61-73: 1.2M cumulative input tokens. Cost: $9.00

The last 13 steps cost more than the first 40 combined. The cost curve isn't linear. It's quadratic. Every step is more expensive than the last because the context keeps growing.

This is why context management isn't a nice-to-have for agent architectures. It's the single biggest lever you have on unit economics. Compress between phases. Drop irrelevant history. Use cheaper models for simple steps.

Or keep appending everything and wonder why your agent workflow costs $18 per run.

posts.title: AI SDRs expose bad ICPs
posts.hook: AI SDRs getting 0.3% reply rates isn't an AI problem. It's a targeting problem that humans were hiding with volume.
posts.body:
AI SDRs getting 0.3% reply rates isn't an AI problem. It's a targeting problem that humans were hiding with volume.

The accounts that score high get sequences. The ones that don't get dropped. No volume play. No spray and pray.

My reply rates aren't high because my copy is better. They're high because I only email people who have a reason to care.

Growth signals: Is the company actually growing, or is the headcount flat? Flat companies don't buy.

Five signal layers. My AI SDR checks all five before a contact enters a sequence. Each signal has a score. Contacts need to clear a threshold. If they don't, they don't get emailed.

posts.title: Dashboards nobody uses
posts.hook: Built a RevOps dashboard last year that took 3 weeks. Usage after 90 days: me, once, to prove it worked.
posts.body:
Built a RevOps dashboard last year that took 3 weeks. Usage after 90 days: me, once, to prove it worked.

The honest truth about dashboards: most of them answer questions nobody is actively asking. They sit there looking professional, refreshing data hourly, while the actual decisions happen in Slack threads and spreadsheets.

What I do now instead:

I build alerts, not dashboards. When a target account visits the pricing page, I get a notification. When a contact's company posts a relevant job opening, it hits my queue. When reply rates on a sequence drop below threshold, the system flags it.

The insight comes to me. I don't go hunting for it.

The second shift: I stopped building for "visibility" and started building for action. Every data point connects to a next step. Account scored above 80? Auto-add to sequence. Contact replied? Create task in CRM. Campaign underperforming? Pause and surface for review.

Dashboards are a coping mechanism for teams that don't trust their automation. If your system is actually working, you don't need to stare at a chart to know it.

The problem isn't the data. It's the delivery mechanism. Dashboards are pull-based. You have to remember they exist, navigate to them, and then figure out what changed. That's three friction points before any insight reaches a decision.

I replaced their entire reporting layer with three things:

A Slack alert that fires when pipeline coverage drops below 3x. A weekly email digest that shows only metrics that moved more than 15% week-over-week. And a Monday morning auto-post in their team channel with the five deals most likely to slip.

No one logs into a dashboard anymore. The data comes to them, pre-filtered, with context. Decisions happen faster because the signal shows up where the conversation already lives.

Stop building views. Start building triggers.

The question got answered in the meeting. The dashboard was the artifact, not the answer.

1. It answers a one-time question dressed up as an ongoing need
2. The person who requested it can't describe what action they'd take if a number changed
3. It requires more than two clicks to reach the insight that matters

What actually works: a single metric piped into the tool your team already lives in. Slack, email, a shared Google Sheet they update weekly anyway. The format matters less than the proximity to the decision.

The best reporting I've ever built looked nothing like a dashboard. It looked like a sentence in a Slack channel.

posts.title: Real personalization vs token personalization
posts.hook: "Hi {first_name}, I noticed {company} is growing fast" is not personalization. It's mail merge with extra steps.
posts.body:
"Hi {first_name}, I noticed {company} is growing fast" is not personalization. It's mail merge with extra steps.

Real personalization requires real research. And real research at scale requires infrastructure.

My enrichment pipeline pulls a contact's recent LinkedIn activity, their company's job postings, tech stack changes, and funding signals before generating a single line of copy. The agent reads all of it, then writes an opener that references something specific.

Not "I see you're hiring." More like "saw you posted a RevOps role focused on attribution modeling. We built something that might make that hire's first week easier."

The difference in reply rates is not subtle. Generic personalization tokens get ignored. Specific, signal-based openers get responses because they prove you actually looked.

But here's the tradeoff nobody mentions: this is slow. Each contact takes 30-45 seconds of compute to enrich and generate. You can't do 500 a day. You do 50. Maybe 80.

And that's fine. 50 well-researched emails outperform 500 templated ones every single time.

Personalization isn't a copy problem. It's a data infrastructure problem.

posts.title: Distribution channels that actually work
posts.hook: $10K MRR with zero paid ads sounds like a flex. It's actually just proof that distribution beats product in the first 12 months.
posts.body:
$10K MRR with zero paid ads sounds like a flex. It's actually just proof that distribution beats product in the first 12 months.

Every solo founder I know who hit early traction did it through some combination of three things:

1. Building in public on one platform consistently (not all of them, one)
2. Showing up in communities where their buyers already ask questions
3. Having one referral loop baked into the product itself

Paid ads work when you've already nailed positioning and have conversion data to optimize against. Before that, you're just burning cash to learn what your landing page should say.

My own distribution is heavily weighted toward Reddit and LinkedIn. Not because they're the best platforms. Because they're where GTM practitioners actually discuss problems. I show up with real build details, not thought leadership. The content does the selling because it demonstrates capability.

The founders who struggle with distribution are usually building in isolation. They ship a great product, then wonder why nobody shows up. Distribution isn't a launch day activity. It's a daily practice that starts before the product is ready.

Your first 100 customers don't come from ads. They come from being useful in the right rooms.

Not two channels. Not a "multichannel strategy." One.

One posted on LinkedIn every single day for 8 months straight. Built a following of exactly the people who buy his product. Never ran a single ad.

Another answered questions on Reddit. Not spammy links, genuine answers with context. Within four months, people started mentioning his tool in threads he wasn't even in.

A third built a referral loop so tight that 40% of new customers came from existing ones. No content, no social presence, just a product that made sharing beneficial for both sides.

The pattern isn't the channel. It's the depth. Every one of these founders resisted the urge to spread across platforms. They said no to TikTok, no to podcasts, no to whatever the latest playbook recommended.

This is counterintuitive because marketing advice tells you to be everywhere. But early-stage distribution is about density, not coverage. You need to be unavoidable in one space, not barely visible in five.

Pick the channel where your buyers already spend time. Show up consistently for 6 months. That's it. That's the strategy.

Spent $0 on ads. Hit $10K MRR in 9 months. Not because paid doesn't work. Because I couldn't afford to learn what works while burning cash.

Paid acquisition has a learning curve measured in dollars. You need to test creatives, audiences, landing pages, and offers. A reasonable test budget is $3-5K before you know if a channel works. For a bootstrapped founder, that's rent.

Organic distribution has a learning curve measured in time. You need to show up, post, engage, iterate, and figure out what resonates. It's slower, but every lesson is free.

The three organic motions that work before you're ready for paid:

1. Build in public on the platform where your buyers already scroll. Show the messy middle, not just wins. People follow process, not polish.

2. Be genuinely useful in communities. Answer questions where your product is relevant. Don't pitch. Help. The pitch becomes obvious when you're consistently the most helpful person in the room.

3. Make your existing users your distribution. A referral program, a case study they're proud to share, a template they send to peers. Turn every customer into a channel.

Paid ads are a multiplier. But you can't multiply zero. Build the organic foundation first, then pour gas on what's already working.

posts.hook: 47 churned users in month 3. Most founders would bury that number. Posting it publicly is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS.
posts.body:
47 churned users in month 3. Most founders would bury that number. Posting it publicly is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS.

Transparency reports work because they do something marketing copy never can: they prove you're paying attention to the hard problems.

When a founder posts "we lost 47 users because onboarding was confusing and we didn't have feature X," two things happen. Prospects see a team that diagnoses problems honestly. And existing users see a team that's likely to fix the thing that's bugging them.

I publish build logs with real numbers. Token costs, pipeline failures, sequences that flopped. Not because vulnerability is a growth hack. Because hiding the failures means never getting external input on fixing them.

The best feedback I've gotten on my GTM engine came from someone who read a post where I admitted my enrichment pipeline was too slow. They suggested a caching layer I hadn't considered. Shipped it that week.

Polished case studies attract tire kickers. Raw transparency attracts practitioners who actually understand what you're building and want to help make it better.

The signal in the noise: founders who share what's broken attract better customers than founders who pretend nothing is.

Three churned users came back. They said seeing us acknowledge the problem and share a fix timeline gave them confidence to retry. Two prospects who were on the fence signed up. Most founders avoid this because it feels risky. What if competitors use it against us? What if prospects get scared off? In practice, the opposite happens. Honesty is so rare in SaaS marketing that it becomes a differentiator by default.

The bar isn't being perfect. The bar is being honest about the gap between where you are and where you're going.
